classification.basis: Complete transection of a main duct (operative history C16; corroborated by ERCP cut-off and MRCP) places the injury in Strasberg type E. The MRCP stump measurement is 25 mm below an intact confluence; C14 Table 2: stump > 2 cm from the confluence = Bismuth I = Strasberg E1. Every other rule is excluded by a named absent finding (no minor-duct leak, no aberrant-duct occlusion/transection/involvement, no lateral injury, confluence intact, stump >= 20 mm), each of which the checker re-evaluates from the findings.

pearls.analysis: Three teaching points, each tied to a scored component. (1) The operative history is evidence — the loudest in the case. 'The injury was recognised and drained' was the learner's reason for discounting it; but drain-and-refer (trace-02, dp4) is a temporising pathway, not a repair: the transected duct was still transected on day 4. The consider-the-opposite prompt (design/07): 'if this is the injury I already know about, what would the stone story have to explain away?' — the clips, the cut-off, and the recognised class III mechanism, at minimum. (2) Sequence the anatomy before the therapy: C14 makes MRCP the gold standard for morphological evaluation and classification of a bile duct injury, and states ERCP's limits in exactly this anatomy — it cannot opacity ducts upstream of a complete obstruction and cannot bridge a transection. Ordered at stage 2 as treatment for an unproven stone, the ERCP is scored non-contributory: it changed no board, no criterion, and no classification input that the record did not already establish, at an invasive procedure's risk. (3) Criteria discipline held where it mattered: TG18 cholangitis reads B and C satisfied but A unmet (afebrile, WBC 8.9, CRP 8) at every stage — not suspected, mechanically — while remaining the case's live risk, which is why the disposition arms surveillance and names the drainage route (PTBD, for complete obstruction) that fever would trigger.
pearls.description: Stage by stage: the workbench leads with the bile duct injury from stage 1 (0.35, its declared prior — the operative history is stage-1 evidence, not backstory) and never gives up the lead. The learner leads with the stone (0.40), raises it on the cholestatic panel (0.45) as if cholestasis discriminated between obstruction causes — it does not; it is shared by all of them — and orders ERCP at stage 2 as therapy, before any cross-sectional anatomy exists. The ERCP returns a cut-off at surgical clips, a clear distal duct, and nothing to treat; the learner still holds the stone at 0.30 ('above the clips, where ERCP cannot see'). Only the stage-4 MRCP closes it: no stone in any duct, and the workbench's one quantified update (LR- 0.0794, C15) carries the stone to 0.0195, across the rule-out line. The learner commits to the injury (0.60) — but still parks 0.25 on the stone, which is the attempt's anchoring event. Learner Brier: 0.7550 -> 0.7118 -> 0.4148 -> 0.2306. The workbench Brier is flat at 0.5150 until the MRCP (0.4053): this case carries exactly one likelihood ratio, and the rest of its reasoning honestly runs through the criteria and classification blocks rather than through invented numbers.
pearls.reactions: The attempt reaches the right diagnosis, the right classification, and the right disposition — and its opening panel (inflammatory markers, cholestasis panel, ultrasound) is exactly the panel C14 prescribes. Between those bookends it commits the error this case was built to expose: it falls for the treatable diagnosis. A retained stone is the cause of postoperative jaundice that ERCP can fix, so the stone is what the learner goes looking for — past an operative history that already contains the answer.
pearls.summary: Diagnosis: major bile duct injury — complete transection of the common bile duct at the index operation (Theatre trace-02), classified by the case's own block from the staged findings as Strasberg E1 / Bismuth I (stump 25 mm below an intact confluence). Disposition as committed: hepatobiliary-centre care, no endoscopic therapy for a transection, Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy after a minimum of 3 weeks (C14 statement 7.4 — the 72 h to 3 week band), cholangitis surveillance meanwhile. Calibration note: a calibration curve is a property of a case SERIES (design/07); the series now has two cases and eight staged learner Brier scores (case 1: 0.4550 -> 0.0276; this case: 0.7550 -> 0.2306 — the gap between those endpoints is, in large part, the price of the anchor), and claims nothing more.
